newsitem.title: USA: Nimo seeks 30-day extension of rate case.
newsitem.headline: Nimo seeks 30-day extension of rate case.

text.p: Niagara Mohawk Power Corp said Wednesday it has requested another 30-day extension of the company's 1997 rate request proceedings.
Last week the parties agreed to a two-week extension, which expires January 21, the utility said.
It said Wednesday's requested extension would postpone filing of staff and intervener testimony until February 20, delaying the effective date any resulting rate change until September 22.
The company said the New York Public Service Commission staff has indicated that it will support the extension.

Niagara Mohawk spokesman Nicholas J. Ashooh said the company's request for further delay had nothing to do with the extended talks on filings in the commission's competitive opportunities case, which includes Nimo's PowerChoice filing.
The utility continues to focus on negotiations with independent power producers, the company's statement said.
If an agreement is reached in those negotiations, the need for the rate case might be eliminated, it noted.
Niagara Mohawk filed the rate case in February 1996 due in part to the rising cost of power it must continue to buy from independent producers if a settlement is not negotiated.
Earlier Wednesday, the utility said it begins 1997 determined to gain regulatory approval for PowerChoice, which Nimo filed with the commission in October 1995.
The regulators accepted PowerChoice, which proposes creation of a competitive electricity market, as Niagara Mohawk's competitive opportunities filing.

As part of its effort to gain approval for PowerChoice and to reduce the cost burdens faced by its customers, Nimo noted, it offered to buy out 44 of the most expensive independent power producer contracts in exchange for cash and securities.
It is this offer that is now being negotiated with owners of these non-regulated generating plants.

PowerChoice calls for the separation of Niagara Mohawk's own electricity generators from the remainder of the company. The company would retain ownership of transmission facilities but would agree to allow an independent, regulated entity -- called an Independent System Operator -- control transmission and ensure all suppliers equal, non-discriminatory access.
Local distribution service would become a Niagara Mohawk subsidiary function and would remain under commission regulation, the utility said.

Marketing and other energy-service functions would compete as unregulated subsidiaries of the parent company. To that end, Niagara Mohawk said, it founded Plum Street Enterprises in 1996 to provide competitive energy services in the Upstate region, a role certain to grow in the coming months.

Plum Street already is engaged in a number of new ventures, including a joint investment with a telecommunications firm to install a fiber-optic network along transmission rights-of-way in Upstate New York.
